subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What are the Earth's layers, listed from the outside inwards?
options: Crust, mantle, outer core, inner core
Mantle, crust, inner core, outer core
Crust, outer core, mantle, inner core
Inner core, outer core, mantle, crust
questions.explain: Moving inwards from the surface, the Earth is made of the crust, the mantle, the liquid outer core and the solid inner core.

questions.q: Which type of crust is thinner and denser?
questions.explain: Oceanic crust is thinner and denser than continental crust, which is why it sinks beneath it at destructive margins.

questions.q: What is the main force that causes tectonic plates to move?
options: The rotation of the Earth on its axis
questions.explain: Heat from the core sets up convection currents in the mantle, which drag the plates above them.

questions.q: At a constructive (divergent) plate margin, the plates are:
questions.explain: At a constructive margin the plates move apart, allowing magma to rise and form new crust.

questions.q: Which feature is formed where two plates move apart beneath an ocean?
questions.explain: As plates move apart under the ocean, rising magma builds a mid-ocean ridge such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.q: The process by which a denser oceanic plate sinks beneath a continental plate is called:
questions.explain: At destructive margins the denser oceanic plate is forced down beneath the continental plate in a process called subduction.

questions.q: Which plate margin has plates sliding past one another, with no crust created or destroyed?
questions.explain: At a conservative margin plates slide past each other, so no crust is made or destroyed but earthquakes still occur.

questions.q: The San Andreas Fault in California is a well-known example of which type of plate margin?
questions.explain: At the San Andreas Fault two plates slide past each other, making it a classic conservative margin.

questions.q: Fold mountains such as the Andes are formed at which type of plate margin?
questions.explain: At destructive margins the collision and subduction of plates crumples sediments upwards to form fold mountains like the Andes.

questions.q: The point underground where an earthquake originates is called the:
questions.explain: The focus is the point beneath the surface where the earthquake begins and energy is first released.

questions.q: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus is called the:
questions.explain: The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus, where shaking is usually strongest.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to detect and record earthquakes?
questions.explain: A seismometer detects and records the seismic waves produced by an earthquake.

questions.q: What does the Richter scale measure?
options: The magnitude, or energy released, of an earthquake
The number of people killed by an earthquake
The depth of the focus below the surface
The visible damage to buildings and roads
questions.explain: The Richter scale is a numerical scale that measures the magnitude, or energy released, of an earthquake.

questions.q: What does the Mercalli scale measure?
options: The intensity of an earthquake based on its effects and damage
The exact energy released at the focus
The speed of the seismic waves
The distance from the epicentre in kilometres
questions.explain: The Mercalli scale measures intensity by describing the observed effects and damage caused by an earthquake.

questions.q: The Richter scale is logarithmic. How much greater is the ground shaking (amplitude) of a magnitude 6 earthquake compared with a magnitude 5?
questions.explain: Because the Richter scale is logarithmic, each whole number increase represents ten times greater ground shaking.

questions.q: A tsunami floods a coastline about an hour after an offshore earthquake. This flooding is best described as:
options: A secondary effect of the earthquake
A primary effect of the earthquake
questions.explain: A tsunami happens as a later consequence of the ground movement, so it is a secondary effect rather than an immediate primary one.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a primary effect of an earthquake?
options: Buildings collapsing due to the ground shaking
Fires breaking out from ruptured gas pipes
Homelessness in the weeks after the event
questions.explain: Primary effects are caused directly by the ground movement itself, such as buildings collapsing during the shaking.

questions.q: Composite (strato) volcanoes are most commonly found at which type of plate margin?
questions.explain: Composite volcanoes form at destructive margins where subducted crust melts to produce viscous, gas-rich magma.

questions.q: Which set of features best describes a shield volcano?
options: Gentle slopes formed from runny, basaltic lava
Steep sides formed from thick, viscous lava
Alternating layers of ash and viscous lava
Violent, explosive eruptions of ash and gas
questions.explain: Shield volcanoes are built by runny basaltic lava that flows a long way, producing wide, gently sloping cones.

questions.q: Why do composite volcanoes tend to erupt more violently than shield volcanoes?
options: Their lava is thick and viscous, so gas and pressure build up
Their lava is very runny and flows away easily
They are always found far from any plate margin
They contain no gas or dissolved water at all
questions.explain: The thick, sticky lava of composite volcanoes traps gas, allowing pressure to build until it is released explosively.

specSource: CCEA GCSE Geography (2017) specification; The Restless Earth
